Marine Hospital Authorities Anxious over San Francisco Cases

The news that three more deaths, thought to have been caused by bubonic plague, in the Chinese quarter of San Francisco, has caused the Marine Hospital authorities to become anxious. Dr. Bailhache, who is Acting Surgeon General in the absence of Dr. Wyman, upon receipt of the report immediately telegraphed to the surgeon in charge of the service at San Francisco asking for details regarding the three cases.

While the authorities at San Francisco do not say that the plague killed the Chinese, they say that the filth and poor sanitary condition of the district have caused an epidemic among the Chinese which may develop into a serious disease. Dr. Bailhache said this morning that it is the general belief that the plague cannot be developed without an original plague germ. He said that if bubonic plague really exists in San Francisco it is most probable that it was brought there from some other country.

If it should be plague, then why was it not prevented from entering the United States? was asked.

There are several ways in which the plague could be brought to San Francisco, replied Dr. Bailhache. Opium is smuggled in, why not plague?

Dr. Bailhache refused to discuss the probabilities at any length, because of the doubtful nature of the reported plague cases. In these three cases the health officers at San Francisco intimate that the cause of the deaths may have been the plague only in a mild form. Glands from the victims are now under examination but no positive verdict has yet been rendered by the bacteriologists at work on them. Every precaution is being taken by the authorities for the preventing of a spread of the disease, and 200 employees of the Health Department have been ordered out to destroy undesirable or dangerous structures in the Chinese district today. "I can only hope for the best," said Dr. Bailhache.

Griffin, Ga. March 24.—Special. 1.—The seventy-eighth annual session of the Georgia State Baptist convention was called to order promptly at 10 o'clock this morning by President W. J. Northen.

Long before the hour for assembling arrived the First Baptist church was crowded to its utmost capacity by the members of the association and delegates.

At 10 o'clock, when the president called for order, nearly every seat in the church was occupied. Governor Northen made a short address to the members and delegates, picturing to them the work of the association in the last year, that which it is now accomplishing and the bright future in store for them.

The president then announced that the first business in order was the election of officers.

Rev. T. N. Galloway, of Wilkes county, arose and moved that the present chairman be re-elected to that position, stating that he had made an excellent officer and a better man could be found for the place. This was unanimously assented to and Governor W. J. Northen was re-elected president of the Georgia Baptist convention to serve during the year ending March, 1901.

The election of secretary was the next thing in order and resulted in the election of Stephens, assistant.

The election of vice presidents resulted in naming the following gentlemen: Rev. H. Walker, of Monroe; Rev. B. S. Dick, of Augusta; Rev. Tom Parks, of Blakely; and Rev. T. W. Hunt, of Macon. The chair announced gentlemen duly elected and requested them to take their seats upon the platform.

Address of Welcome.

Rev. J. D. Gruss, Griffin, was then introduced to the audience and the address of welcome was delivered. He said he had intended to make an exceedingly warm address of welcome, but had been so very busy for the past two weeks that he was unable to prepare anything.

Introduced as speaker in response to the address of welcome, and said in brief terms, he had heard and appreciated the words of the pastor. He was here seventeen years ago and that meeting was one to remember. He reviewed the instant events that had transpired since that meeting that were the outcome of all previous meetings. He said it was not needed another big meeting to stir things up and hoped many blessings would result from the present assembly.

The reports of the standing committees were then called for, and the various committees that had not already held meetings made their reports ready for reading. Immediately retired.

Mercer University Report.

The report of the trustees of Mercer University was a lengthy one, but full of interest. The report has the following:

Again, our ranks have been invaded, and one of the modest heroes of our alumni has laid aside his armor and an empty roll remains. We mourn the loss of our dearly beloved brother, Dr. Parker. During the year we have received some magnificent gifts. Brother Parker, Sister Reynolds, and Sister Wilggs has been added as an additional sister. And others interested in this great work we have reviewed also. There is ready to be transferred from the Cheney estate in Illinois to the association already received, estimated by the executors, worth $9,000, making $9,000 received since last year.

During this year the following honorary degrees were conferred: Doctor of Laws upon E. Henry, president of Clemson College, South Carolina; Hon. Emory Sucer, dean of our law department; and Hon. J. E. Black, of Augusta, Degree of Doctor of Divinity upon Brethren R. W. O'Kelley, of Atlanta, and D. Jordan, of Savannah.

E. Y. MALLORY, secretary.

Broughton's Resolution.

Broughton addressed the convention for twenty minutes on prohibition and much interest was manifested throughout the audience. He was in a circle of the church taking hold of politics and criticizing all politicians. He said he was not an honest politician.

Broughton said a first class fight is the best thing this convention can put during its session.

Broughton was followed by several other ardent supporters of prohibition. They raised their voices for prohibition, and it was apparent from the interest being taken in the question that the convention would have this the leading topic throughout.

Broughton is among the strong friends of prohibition. He spoke, asking all to stand by him. The cause is not long in Georgia, but at present were not in a position to win. Dr. Woods said he had a good idea of a useful amendment to Broughton's resolution, making it read: "white democratic voters."

Grant, 41 years old, and David King, 35
years, both of the town of Clarksburg, were
arrested to-day on the charge of murdering
Henry F. Reed and his sister Blanche
Reed, in their house in this city on the
morning of August 2, 1897.

The closing session of the inquest that has
been in continuance during the last two and
one-half years, was held here to-day, at
which District Attorney Gardner of Spring-
field was present. Grant and King, who
have been on the stand numerous times,
were again put on the stand to-day. Grant
was first examined, and was permitted to
go, but was immediately arrested. King,
who was examined at the inquest to-day,
subsequent to Grant, was not permitted to
leave the courtroom.

arrest.

his arrest. They will be arraigned Monday
morning in the District Court for Northern
Berkshire. Officers were immediately dis-
patched to the men's homes in Clarksburg
to guard the premises, in anticipation of a
thorough search, which will be made under
the direction of Officer Dunham, the hope
being to find some articles that may have
belonged to the Reed house.

Washington, June 13.—Official dispatches

received in diplomatic quarters here show that the
rioting in Peking has reached an acute stage,
with the rioters directing number of their
assaults against members of the foreign legations
there. One of these dispatches says that the
Secretary of the Belgian Legation attacked
twice on Monday, and escaped after being badly
treated by the mob. It is said that the Belgian
secretary probably Philip May, formerly
with the Belgian Legation in Washington, and
well known in social and official circles here.
On the same day two officials of the British
Legation serving student interpreters, were
attacked. The young Englishmen held the at-
tacking party back for a time, but when the
mob threatened to close in on them they drew
revolvers, and by show of force effected their
retreat without injury. About the same time
the British summer quarters, fourteen miles
from Peking burned. These quarters were
extensive and had just been completed. They
belonged to the British Government and not to
Sir Claude Macdonald, the British Minister at
Peking, which gives added significance to the
depreciation.

The killing of the chancellor of the Japanese
Legation at Peking, Sugiyama Akira, is not
mentioned in the official dispatches received
here but full credit is given to the report by the
Japanese officials who were acquainted with Mr.
Akira and with many of the circumstances
related. The killing of a member of the diplo-
matic body and the assaults the officials of
foreign countries regarded presenting the
most serious phase of the situation.

The Japanese Charge d'Affaires in Washing-
ton, Keiziro Nabeshima, said to-day:
We have no official confirmation of the killing
of the chancellor at Peking but there appears
to be no doubt of the fact, and it presents a most
serious condition. The chief offence is against
Japan, but aside from that it is against the
entire diplomatic body at Peking, for if any one of
them is subject to assaults, the others
share in the same danger. I was personally ac-
quainted with Mr. Akira, as he served with me
in the division of protocols; he was a bright
young man, about thirty-eight years old, and
had a wife and four children. He was one of the
most expert calligraphers in Japan, and this
gained him the post of chancellor at Peking
where he went about three years ago.

Mr. Nabeshima said that the Japanese Gov-
ernment had pursued the utmost reserve up to
this time, not wishing to be open to any
suspicions, but he felt that if this tragedy had
occurred, energetic action would be taken. One of
the most significant features of the affair in his
judgment, is that the killing was reported to
have been done by the troops of the Empress
Dowager, and not by any lawless mob. While
there might be excuse for mob depreda-
tions, Mr. Nabeshima said, it would be difficult
to take any favorable view of an attack by
Chinese soldiers against the officials of foreign Gov-
ernments.

A cable dispatch has been received at the
State Department from Minister Conger saying
that Tuan, the father of the heir apparent, has
been appointed president of the Tsung-Yamen;
also that three other Ministers have been
appointed, all affiliated with the party opposed
to foreigners. On the whole Mr. Conger re-
ports the situation is not materially improved.
Guards are repairing the railway, and soon
as they have arrived at Peking it is Mr. Con-
ger's belief that the safety of the foreigners
there will be assured.

The State Department has heard nothing offi-
cially about the reported killing of an American
missionary. The report caused shock at the
Department; it is realized that this adds
greatly to the gravity of the problem awaiting
settlement.

WASHINGTON, April 20.—The House Committee on an Interstate and Foreign Commerce to-day made an important change to the Hepburn Nicaragua canal bill, striking out the provision for the "fortification" and thus providing what is said to be a compromise which will aid in bringing the measure to an early consideration.

The amendment was proposed by Representative Barham of California. The committee was instructed to report on consideration of the bill at the proper time as committee amendment thereto.

The amendment was agreed to, notwithstanding some expressions of reluctance, but with a view to overcoming opposition AND securing action. In its new form, the section reads as follows:

"Sec 1. Be it enacted, etc., That the President of the United States be, and is, authorized to acquire from the states of Costa Rica and Nicaragua for and in behalf of the United States control of such portion of territory now belonging to Costa Rica and Nicaragua as may be desirable and necessary on which to excavate, construct, and protect a canal of such depth and capacity as will be sufficient for the movement of ships of the greatest tonnage and draft now in use, from point near Greytown on the Caribbean sea, via Lake Nicaragua, to Brito, on the Pacific coast; and such sum as may be necessary to secure such control is hereby Appropriated out of any money in the treasury not otherwise appropriated.

"Sec 2 That when the President has secured full control over the territory in section 1 referred to, he shall direct the Secretary of War to excavate and construct a canal and waterway from a point on the shore of the Caribbean sea, near Greytown, by way of Lake Nicaragua to a point near Brito, on the Pacific OCEAN. Such canal shall be of sufficient capacity and depth as that it may be used by vessels of the largest tonnage, and greatest depth now in use, and shall be supplied with all necessary locks and other appliances to meet the necessities of vessels passing from Greytown to Brito, and The Secretary of War shall also construct such safe and commodious harbors at the termini of said canal, and such provision for defense, as may be necessary for the safety and protection of said canal and harbors."

Mr. Hepburn then announced that it had been definitely arranged that the House would take up the canal bill on May 1 and Mr. Hepburn says the passage of the bill is unquestionable.

The main dissent to the change in the bill came from Mr. Adamson of Georgia, who desired to have the words "fortify and defend" retained, as against any doubtful or compromising phraseology. Mr. Barham, upon whose motion in the committee the changes in the bill were effected, said:

"On the amended form ample authority is given to police and protect the canal against destruction by evildoers, and by the time the canal is completed, six or eight years hence, there will be full opportunity to determine whether the canal should be permanently protected by fortification or by our navy. For the present we avoid a needless issue in no way bearing on the main question of constructing the waterway."

The minority report filed by Mr. Shackleford of Missouri, says:

"The act should contain an explicit and direct assertion of the right of the United States to build, own and control said canal, absolutely free from European dominion.

The Clayton-Bulwer treaty long ago ceased to have any binding force by reason of the conduct of Great Britain. That being true we should strictly adhere to the Monroe doctrine and stand by our traditional policy that Europe will not be permitted to intermeddle with Central American affairs. It is to the Monroe doctrine that we, as a republic, must look for safety."

ticipated in these meetings were Senators

Committee on Naval Affairs.

Revenue law Senators Aldrich, Allison

Representatives Payne and Dalzell of the

no conclusion had been reached. So far

their expression were favorable to making
the revision so thorough as to relieve the
work entirely of the possibility of having
it considered of temporary character
They expressed the opinion that what

made at the present session in order
TO prevent the re-opening of the subject
at the next session of Congress, as they
think that if the question should be en-,
tered upon at the beginning of a long
session an entire revision of the tariff
might be attempted. This they would
avoid. They also gave some indication

in a general way favoring the removal

turning a large revenue and leaving it

uous effort to have this measure made

man enough to break a heart as loyal
as Amy's?"

"Don't get tragic, Tom. I'm not go-
ing to break anybody's heart. Nell is
rich, you know."

"And so are you," sneered Fair-
leigh, walking hurriedly to the door
and laying his hand on the knob, "but
Amy Hepburn is poor. Society dares
you to wed with poverty. If you love
Amy, are you man enough to dare?
Examine into the financial condition
of the Hepburns, reflect upon what
caused their downfall in fortune and
then let me see if you are strong
enough to leap this Brahminical bar-
rier of caste."

With this parting shot Fairleigh
passed quickly out of the room and
slammed the door behind him. Harry
Gordon gave vent to a long whistle,
seated himself back in chair and
thoughtfully lighted a cigar.

"That was quite a JOLT!" he muttered,
looking upward through the curling
wreaths of smoke. "How happy could
I be with either were t'other charmer
away! It's as sure as can be that I
love one and fancy the other. But
who will unravel this Gordian knot?
Which is it to be—Amy or Nell?"

A knock fell on the door, not on the
outside door, but on a door leading in
to a closet. Harry Gordon stirred
himself comfortably in his chair, a vexed look
coming into his eyes as he fixed them
upon the closet door. After a brief
interval of silence the knock was re-
peated.

"Now, what in the world?" cried Gordon.

"Business is business," came a hol-
low voice from the other side of the
closet door. "I'm here for a purpose,
and if I do not make that purpose
manifest once in a while you'll forget
all about me—"

This remark was followed by a
clanking, cachinnatory outburst that
seemed to grate harshly on Gordon's
ear.

"Well, what do you want?" he asked.

"I want to come out and show my-
self. You know I'm here, but a little
ocular demonstration won't come
amiss, take it. Remember, I'm show-
ing consideration for you. I might
have kicked open this door and stalked
out into the room. But I didn't. I rapped."

"Can't you put it off? Come out to-
morrow. I've got something else to
think about now."

"The high and mighty order of fam-
ily skeletons are not in the habit of
playing second fiddle or taking back
seats for anybody. I'm coming at
once."

"All right, then," groaned Gordon,
squirming himself about on his chair.
"Come on."

The closet door flew open and
a well developed skeleton strode out and
dropped with a rattle into a chair. The
cavernous eyes were blankly express-
ive to Gordon. For him also there
was something sarcastic in the grin
of the skeleton.

"Dust me off," said the skeleton. "I
want to show up as frightful as possi-
ble tonight."
The request presented itself to Cor-
don as a command which he was pow-
erless to disobey. Picking up a feath-
er duster, he piled it vigorously about
the cleaning white bones.

"Achoo!" he sneezed, dropping the
duster and falling into his chair.

"You ought not to neglect me—" said the skeleton. "I'm one of the family
and should be treated as such. Now,
then, let's have a chat."

The skeleton crossed its bony legs
and settled back comfortably.

"Will it do me any good to have a
chat with you?" queried Gordon.

"That remains to be seen. It used
to do your father good. Why, it was
my custom to visit him every night.
As he sat before that table writing"

A result there is "a hue and cry" on the part of people of the North, about what they term the unwarranted discrimination against the colored race. Kennebunk, Me. Nov. 25—The fast
St. John express, known as the "Sunrise
express" from St. John, N.B., for
Boston, collided with an eastbound
freight train near the Kennebunk sta-
tion at 10 o'clock this morning, and
although both engines were badly dam-
aged and several cars smashed, none of
the passengers or trainmen were seri-
ously injured. Two locomotives were
derailed and these with the portions of
disabled cars piled up along the track,
blocked traffic for several hours on the
main line, but the sidtrack soon was
opened and the regular running of
trains resumed. The express, which
does not stop at this place, was run
at high speed when the collision
occurred, and it is considered almost
miraculous that no fatalities resulted.
The eastbound freight had been set
off on a sidtrack. The engine had
just returned from down the main line,
with several loaded box cars and was
backing in on the switch when the ex-
press came bowling down. The engi-
neer of the express attempted to run
on full power and attempted to make
the siding before the express reached
him, and he nearly succeeded in doing
this, as only the forward half of the
engine was on the main line when the
express dashed in. The heavy engine
of the express struck the freight loco-
motive partly on its pilot and partly
on the side and both were thrown from
the iron. The baggage car, one Pul-
man and a passenger car were thrown
from the rails, considerably smashed
and piled up beside the track, but the
occupants were uninjured save for
general shaking up. Each locomotive
was damaged to the extent of several
thousand dollars, and all three of the
derailed cars will require extensive re-
pairs before they again are ready for
use. The responsibility for the collision
has not been placed.

 A review of the acts of last winter will best explain the situation. In New York no minor under IS can now be employed in a factory, and no woman can be employed before o'clock in the morning and after o'clock at night. In Nebraska females can not be employed longer than ten hours a day. In Rhode Island ten hours is made the limit of a days work by women and by children under 16 years of age. In Michi- gan children cannot be employed at night In Wisconsin persons under IS can work but eight hours day in cigar factories, and no person under 16 can be employed longer than ten hours in any factory, and such persons cannot be employed at night. Children under IA cannot be employed at all. In Indiana no person under 16 and no female under IS can work more than ten hours a day. No children under IA can be employed no woman can be employed at night, and no minor can be employed to clean machinery while in motion.

 The health and moral surroundings of the young and weak are carefully safeguarded in such legislation. and the Woman's Fed eration is doing a wonderful and blessed work in this direction. But there are forty five States in the Union. and much work remains to be accomplished. Instead of seeking the suffrage the women of the fed eration are striving to secure helpful and humane legislation, and their success in the past is a guarantee of still greater suc- cess in the future.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal


WASHINGTON, Feb. 24.—The investigation of the bribery charges against Senator Clark, of Montana, is rapidly drawing to a close. Within a few days the taking of evidence will cease and the committee will begin to hear the argument of counsel. Senator Hoar thinks that within two weeks all will be over so that the committee will begin to sum up evidence and argument with a view to agreeing on report. The Daily side is now having its inning, John K. Toole, close friend of Mr. Clark's rival, having been heard to-day. He denied all the charges made by the senator's witnesses. Probably no investigation in the history of Congress has developed such a remarkable mass of testimony as this case. The volume and the character of it are wonderful. Somehow in the course of the hearing there has been an unprecedented mass of perjury and it will be surprising if the result of the case does not affect Montana politics for years to come.


In the preliminary stages of the investigation the testimony was all against Clark and men wondered how a man guilty of the crimes charged against him could have the hardihood to expect a seat in the United States Senate. Everything appeared against him. Since the witnesses for the defense began testifying, it has become apparent there were two sides to the question and those who at first were certain the millionaire senator was an arch-corruptionist have had ample occasion to change their minds to the extent of accepting the view that Mr. Marcus Daily has been engineering a remarkable political conspiracy against his old business and political enemy who now holds the seat from Montana.


Senator Clark has proved manifest advantage in the character of the witnesses who have testified for him. As a rule they appeared to be men of character and standing and in no important instance has any serious attempt been made by the prosecution to impeach their testimony. On the other hand, the witnesses for the prosecution have included men who were willing to testify to anything to maintain their point. On more than one occasion, members of the committee have spoken out during the investigation and stated that the prosecuting testimony was of such a character that no intelligent men would give it any credence.


The turning point in the case came with the testimony of Senator Clark. He flatly denied having, in a single instance, used money to purchase votes. He admitted having put up all the money for the campaign to elect the Democratic ticket which involved large sums for campaign orators, bands, torchlight processions, railroad expenses, hotel bills and such expenses, and he showed that in a State of such magnificent distances it was easy to spend an enormous sum of money. It was apparent, too, that a great horde of campaigners were industriously engaged from the beginning in testing the ductility of his leg. Senator Clark was recognized as a good spender and they never lost sight of an opportunity to touch him. But he denied having even indirectly negotiated for votes and even the prosecution has never been able to prove he had.


As the matter stands, the case must necessarily hinge largely on the senator's own testimony. He is member of the club, so to speak, and the committee will be likely to extend to him the senatorial courtesy of accepting his statements against the indefinite testimony of witnesses, many of whom were self-confessed boodlers. In reaching the final conclusion the committee, while disposed to throw away the great mass of irrelevant testimony, it will unquestionably condemn the Montana methods of political manipulation. That there has been unprecedented mass of rottenness in that State is patent.

County.

cial committee. These plus will fail
to the counties less continuously repre-
sented in the patronage list. Mercer, Atlantic, Camden

each while Salem, Cape May, Gloucester, Ber-
gen and Essex will receive one each.

was in the Assembly in 1819, 1822 and 1824.

ley are appointments.

Tuesday morning. After the caucus to-day the

tor Johnson.

Of Interest to State Banks Converted

Into National Ones.

WASHINGTON, D. C., May 18.—A decision of much interest to state banks already converted or about to be converted into national banks has just been rendered by the commissioner of Internal Revenue in response to an inquiry concerning the Bank of Holland Patent, New York, as to whether it would have to pay the special tax second time on becoming nationalized. The collector rules that "the bank's name is changed without affecting its identity, and it has the same capital, the same officers, and the same stockholders, doing business uninterruptedly under a change of jurisdiction, retaining its right to sue upon obligations or liabilities incurred to it by its former name. It is held to be one and the same bank which has already paid its special tax, and another special tax is not required."

In most, and possibly in all cases where state banks have undergone conversion in this manner, the local collectors have served notice upon them that they must pay the special tax as if they were new institutions beginning business. improvement of James River and hopes
to get the 100,000 appropriation from
congress which the Council Committee on
Improvement of James River has asked
for. Every member of this committee
feels confident that the appropriation
will be made at the next session of Con-
gress. This money will be employed in
charging the Richmond harbor, deepening
the channel, and improving the river.

MR. WALLENSTEIN FOR CHEAP GAS

The movement started by Mr. Joseph
Wallenstein about a year ago to reduce the
price of gas used by the residents of the
city from 81 to 50 cents per 1000 feet has
been revived and resolution to make the
price lower is now awaiting the consid-
eration of the Council Committee on
Lights. This resolution, if adopted, will
reduce gas bills about 20 per cent in
many instances. When the price of gas is
reduced it is thought that hundreds of
housekeepers, the hotels and restaurants
of the city will also use it freely for cooking
purposes. Many of the members of the
Council are reported as being heartily in
favor of the reduced price of gas and its
use for cooking purposes.

The new machinery and engines now
being put in at the gas works will afford
a larger supply of gas and make the plant
one of the most efficient in the coun-
try. Mr. W. X. Knowles, the superintend-
ent, is very much encouraged over the
progress made thus far in improving the
gas works.

IMPROVING THE PARKS

One of the many things the Council
Committee on Grounds and Buildings has
considered during the past two months
was a method for improving the parks of
the city and putting them in a creditable
condition. Already contracts have been
let for putting hydrants in the parks for
the purpose of sprinkling the various sec-
tions. It is proposed to keep each of the
parks verdant and beautified.

Mr. Henry J. Beck, as a member of
the Council Committee on Cemeteries, is
interesting himself in the improvement of
Shadloe Hill Cemetery. He wants to get
an appropriation from the city so as
to proceed with improving the cemetery at
once. Mr. Beck asked Mr. George B.
Davis if he could not put some of the
men he had as inmates at the almsh
houses to work in the cemetery. Mr.
Davis said that he put two of the old
men out at work, withdrawing a fence
and that they died after completing the
work. He did not think that he could use
the inmates on such work.

THE TRASH BOXES.

The movement is now in progress to have
trash boxes placed on the street corners of
the city and it is sanctioned by the presi-
dent of the Board of Health, Dr. W. T.
Oppenheimer, the Committee on Health
and some of the members of the City
Council. Dr. Oppenheimer thinks that the
boxes would tend to improve the sanitary
condition of the city. These boxes will
be used for holding waste paper, fruit
peelings and other waste material not
properly called garbage. Garbage con-
sists of kitchen refuse, dead animals,
combustibles, waste, animal and vegetable
refuse, condemned food and waste mate-
rial on cook-rooms.

The Council Committee on Health is now
planning methods for improving the
streets of the city from sanitary stand-
point and will do a great deal of work
along this line.

Special from Emporia, Kan. says, Hundreds of men on foot, on horseback, and in all kinds of vehicles, are securing Emporia valley tonight for two alleged bank robbers James Murphy and Z. Estel, who last night added murder to their crime by killing Deputy Marshal Edward Roberts and Dunlap, a member of a party that had been pursuing the robbers for several days.

The bridegroom opportunity had come. But the Church had her lamp untrimmed. A chaplain with raucous voice discoursed on the details of the siege and surrender of Jericho. The soldiers froze into apathy, and after a while the formal, perfunctory service reached its welcome conclusion. As I marched home officer said to me: 'Why is it, when the Church spends so much on missionary work among heathens, she does not take the trouble to send good men to preach in time of war?'"

Of course, it is wholly impossible to defend a Church which sends to the front men whose voice is disparaged by one of the war correspondents; and I am not going to attempt to justify clergyman for selecting a theme of battle when he addresses a multitude of soldiers.

What seems to me a great pity is that this respondent happened upon this clergyman upon the Sunday, and a greater pity is that he should have drawn upon this single case an indictment against all the clergy who are with our armies.

For my part I found no lack of good men in Methuen's army, and have not yet noticed a departure from the rule in Lord Roberts's immediate command. Some of who have been attached to the western forces all the time have more than once had occasion to call attention to the jealous, ungrateful mob, work not only the regular commissioned Chaplains who are with us, but of the volunteer clergy as well.

There has, it is true, been some kindly discernment among the onlookers as to whether it becomes men to advance with the troops into the heat of battles to minister to the dying while bullets shredded the air and other men were falling around them. For we have chaplains who have done this, and chaplains who have served as gallopers, dashing in and out of awful danger in the worst of all engagements. This was only when one must and there one else. Perhaps they should have stayed at the hospitals—it is not for me to say—but only think now how it must be for men who have literally shouldered Death aside in Haiti to reach the soldiers' heart in their hour.

We have had not only fighting chaplains, but chaplains who have valiantly remained in the near rear to succor the wounded and dying as fast as they were brought out of the volcanoes of shot and shell; we have enjoyed the sermons of both sorts, for both have chosen their themes and arguments to suit and to stir the soldier mind; but I do not remember to have known or heard of a single chaplain who deserves the reflected gloom which his gifted comrades' criticism is said to have cast back upon them all.

A large outside interest was manifest, and the professional operators who bought at the lower level were busy in bidding up the prices of their holdings and in feeding the new demand to take their profits; but while selling stocks from the one hand to realize on the rise they were mixing in new holdings of different stocks with the other. The duration of this kind of upward movement does not always depend strictly on the continuance of the public demand for stocks. ees, the hearers, the Democrats, the bosses,


were doing the work that these old fell-


ows were to swallow later on.


At 2:15 the convention reconvened and


committee reports were received and


adopted.


The report of the committee on creden-


tials disclosed no report or delegation


from Gray, Greeley, Haskell, Kiowa, Lane,


or Stanton.


The committee on permanent organiza-


tion recommended Sam Hale of Rush for


permanent chairman.


Hale declared himself a Republican and


said he always had been. Since 1892 he


said, he had been a Silver Republican


and was proud of it.


"I was fortunate enough," he said, "to


be the delegate to the Minneapolis national


Republican convention of 1892. In that


convention I supported McKinley, and


in that connection I want to say I have


some documents I used in support of


McKinley which I will use in this cam-


paign."


Hale took up the silver question and


claimed that President McKinley made


the money question the paramount one in


this campaign. He referred to Long in


one particular when he said: "In a speech


Long made at Garden City the other day,


he said if the president and his admin-


istration were reelected they would do


thus and so. I said to the boys at home


and said I didn't know but McKinley


would be willing to do certain things,


but I didn't think the administration


would let him."


Hale then hammered away on trusts, but failed to explain why the Democrats


did not assist last session of Congress in


passing an amendment giving Congress


power to restrict, restrain, control or


abolish all trusts and combinations.


In the midst of Hale's speech T. J.


Crotts of Reno again interrupted the


proceedings and suggested that "this was


not the time or the occasion to consume


all the afternoon in speaking."


This did not faze Hale in the least,


and he whaled away again at imperial-


ism. In this connection Hale mentioned


the fact that he now had a son fighting


in the Philippines.


Asher of Reno then suggested that


Webb McNall again address the conven-


tion with the understanding that he could


when any committee showed up. Amidst


loud cheers Webb took the platform, but


he hadn't proceeded very far when a


committee came in. Webb sloshed around


generally and amused the crowd.


Senator W. A. Harris was introduced!


Following McNall, Senator Harris, after


relating some historic facts, such as Nel-


son's injunction to his men at Trafalgar,


and Napoleon's to his men when he told


them that forty centuries looked down


on them, said: "Every man in Kansas is


watching and praying for a successful


result of this convention. Not alone


that, but 125 years of self-government is


in the balance, and watching the result


and the manner in which you consider


the serious question which you have to


decide.


I beg of you to act with calmness and


moderation. For the past four hours this


has troubled me. You do not know that


your action will control in the nation.


The Seventh district always has been


considered the tenth legion in fusion


forces and I beg of you, do not turn


away from your banners, shunning


away the eagles of victory from your


banners by hasty or injudicious action."


The senator took up the Porto Rican
tariff and dwelt upon it at great length,
and trusts, as well.


Judge Ray of Wichita presented the
resolutions. The points were:


1-Endorsement of the Sioux Falls plat-
form and Kansas City candidates and
Fort Scott platform and candidates.


2-Approve the action of Duval and
Campbell in retiring from the race for


Chester I. Long for voting
for the ship subsidy bill, which is all
right except that the bill never came
from committee during the session.


Various other things were suggested,
such as digging up some old Republican
platforms.


When Ray had completed the reading
of the resolutions, Charley Blakesley,
correspondent for the Kansas City Times,
asked Ray if he might have a copy.


"I haven't but one copy," said Ray, in a
surely tone.


Blakesley then suggested that he
might look over the copy, but Ray didn't
want to let them set away, so Blakesley
said if Ray thought that the best dispos-
ition of the platform, he didn't care.


Senator Harris resumed his speech fol-
lowing the reading of the resolutions.
The committee of conference reported through C. W. Fairchilds, as follows:


We recommend that both conventions
meet in the A. O. L. W. hall at 8 o'
clock and that the members who are
found duly accredited by the
credential committee, each convention
entitled to seats in the joint conven-
tion in naming a choice for Congressman
from this district it shall require, etc.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 3.—Senator Foraker to-day introduced a bill providing a form of government for the Island of Porto Rico. The bill provides for the continuance of the laws and municipal ordinances now in force in the island until the Legislature provided for shall supplant them. The President is empowered to appoint a Governor and a Supreme Court, and also seven heads of departments to have charge of the various interests of the government and also five native citizens who, together with the Governor and heads of departments, are to constitute the upper branch of the insular Legislature. A lower house of thirty-five members, to be elected by the citizens of the island, is also provided for, and all inhabitants of the island are made citizens of the United States. The citizens are also to elect a delegate to Congress, who is to have a seat, but no vote. The island is to be divided into twelve districts for judicial and legislative purposes and each district is to have a local court, to consist of such a number of judges as the Legislature may provide for.

The Constitution and laws of the United States are extended to the island, so far as the latter are locally applicable. Export duties are prohibited and free trade is provided for between the island and United States proper. Articles imported into Porto Rico from the United States are to pay the same duties as those imposed in the ports of this country. The money thus collected is to go into the island treasury, but money raised by revenue collections is to be covered into the national treasury of the United States. A commission of five members, two of whom are to be natives, is provided for to revise the system of laws and of judicial procedure in the island. For the present no franchises are to be provided, except on the approval both of the Governor of the island and the President of the United States.

Speaking of the bill, Senator Foraker said it did not create a Territory out of the island, nor undertake to give the island a territorial form of government in the ordinary understanding of that phrase, adding that it merely provided a simple form of government, which, it is believed, would answer the purpose until a more mature form could be devised. The senator also said that the bill was intended only as a basis for the committee on Porto Rico, to act upon.

Late developments have made it plain to the Democratic county committee, however, that the voters of Commissioner Boyce's district have long memories and that a blunder has been made that is now impossible of correction.

Four years ago James H. Boyce, now a member of the board of county commissioners and a candidate for re-election on the Democratic ticket, was supervisor of a county road district in the north district. He then resided in that district.

More than four years ago Road Supervisor Boyce was guilty of a malfeasance in office whereby the county road fund was defrauded. Before the crime was discovered Road Supervisor Boyce became the nominee of the fusion party for the office of county commissioner from the north district, and was in November 1896 elected to that office.

At the time of his election and before Supervisor Boyce had assumed the duties of the office to which he had been chosen by the voters of his party, he was publicly charged by the leading fusionist newspaper of Seattle, and of the state of Washington, that he, with others, was more than suspected of serious frauds against the county road and bridge fund.

On the first Monday in January, 1897, Mr. Boyce in the courthouse in this city took the oath of office and assumed the duties of county commissioner as a member of the reform administration swept into office by the Populist landslide of 1896.

Experts Discover Crookedness.

Less than two months after that date experts employed by the newly elected county auditor brought to light the fact that by the dishonesty of two officers of the county administration, County Commissioner W. N. Heaton, Populist, and Deputy County Auditor Levi Q. Smith, a Republican who had acted as clerk of the board of county commissioners, the county road and bridge fund had been defrauded out of many thousands of dollars, that the supervisors of dozen or more of the road districts of the county had been implicated in the frauds, and that County Commissioner Boyce was one of the guilty parties.

At that time the Seattle organ of Commissioner Boyce's party printed in its news columns the facts regarding the road and bridge fund scandal and in the editorial paragraph quoted heretofore called upon Commissioner Boyce to cleanse his hands by the act of resigning the office to which he had been elected.

A year later Judge Henson, of the Superior Court, himself a fusionist, called a special grand jury to investigate the frauds against the road and bridge fund, and indicted Commissioner Boyce, who had confessed his crime and refunded the money stolen from the county treasury, but who had nevertheless refused to resign his office. The pressure brought upon him from every side was great.

The records of the criminal department and the Superior Court to-day show that Mr. Heaton and Smith were jointly indicted for this crime, obtaining money by false pretenses, that they were arrested and placed under bond, at $5,000 each, and that owing to legal difficulties in the prosecution of the said case, with many others of similar character, was never brought to trial and justice was suffered a die for lack of prosecution.

Commissioner Boyce claims to be innocent for all intents and purposes; the same can also be said of him that it was less than four years since the official organ of his party advised him to cleanse his hands by resigning his office. No one has ever heard the charges against him and, indeed, a great number of citizens and taxpayers have even declared their belief in his guilt.

Despite of this, however, as Boyce is a candidate for re-election, the Democratic party is supporting this official after his record.

The only excuse Commissioner Boyce has ever offered for his candidacy, "a baseless fraud against the taxpayers of King county," that he was as innocent as a child. The fault in this case was upon Commissioner Heaton who at that time was not a political partisan. Commissioner Heaton went away after the very first case.

Fighting then a lieutenant, with a handful of men, defended one corner of the mountain top amid a fierce fusillade from the Boer rifles, with dead and wounded comrades lying about him, and when at length the end of that bitter and terrible struggle came it found him prisoner. The Board of Library Trustees has submitted to the Commissioners its report of work done during the year. The report is largely devoted to the new Carnegie Library building, and in part says:

"A contract has been made with Richardson & Burgess of this city, for the erection of the building complete, and equipped with all apparatus—excepting bookstacks, elevator, lighting fixtures, and furniture—for the sum of $277,900, which, with the cost of the omitted items, foundation work, commissions to architects and superintendent of construction, and miscellaneous expenses, will exhaust the $4,000,000 donated for public library purposes by Mr. Andrew Carnegie.

The building is to consist of a rectangular central pavilion 113 feet and 9 inches long (north and south) and 90 feet ten inches broad, with equal wings, east and west, respectively, each 63 feet 9 inches long (north and south) and 81 feet 10 inches broad. The building is to stand in the centre of Mt. Vernon Square, but nearly seven-eighths of Mt. Vernon Square are untouched by the new building and the park space available for public use is upon the ground upon which the best trees are growing.

The basement is but partly below the ground level. Its central pavilion is occupied by the entrance hall and bicycle room, the lavatories, packing-room, and receiving rooms. The east wing is devoted to store rooms. In the west wing the basement is one entire room not yet assigned. This may ultimately become the children's reading-room.

In the first or principal story the general delivery hall behind the long delivery counter for the service of books to readers is a wide passage to the book stack that occupies the whole north end of this pavilion, extending up through both the first and second stories. The east wing is used as the general public reading-room and the west wing is divided equally by partition between the children's reading room and the main open shelf room. In the second story the central pavilion contains a memorial or exhibition hall, several private study rooms and the trustees room. The east wing in this story contains the public reading-room for periodicals and newspapers, and the west wing may also be used as a reading-room, but is designed as a lecture or classroom. There are altogether thirty-six rooms and halls.

The exterior stone work is somewhat smaller than originally proposed, but of a good quality of white marble, and the Milford pink granite for the basement is retained. The roof will be covered with black slate, with the sheet metal work thereon of galvanized iron, and the gutters, flashings, and net portions are to be copper.

White marble is retained for the stairways, but all other interior marble finish is omitted. It is expected that the funds will permit a pleasing color treatment for the interior walls. The building will be fireproof throughout.

The book racks will have a capacity of about 254,500 volumes. The present library contains less than 150,000 volumes. While they overflow the shelves of the building now in use, they will be lost in the structure in Mount Vernon Square. The special labor of all friends of the library will be to so increase the number of volumes on its list that the shelves of the new building, at least so far as the first floor is concerned, may be filled when the library enters its new quarters.

The creation of a circulating department of the Library of Congress has been forcibly urged in Congress, but has met with determined opposition. A compromise between these views of the true functions of the Library of Congress should result in the popular circulating use of many of these books through their loan to the Washington Public Library."

An examination of the printed testimony taken before the Senate Committee on Pensions is very interesting.

The first witness was the Secretary of the Interior Hon. E. H. Hitchcock who said that he held the Office since Feb. 20, 1899. He knew that there were such things as Orders No. 161 and 225, but was not familiar with their practical or administrative operation. He had heard that some had claimed that Order 161 was too liberal, and that others claimed that Order 225 was altogether too restrictive, but I am told by The Commissioner that in practical operation there is no difference at all—that is, in the matter of rating disabilities. That is the keynote of the whole matter.

This confirms what we have previously said about the pension business. The Secretary himself relies wholly on the Commissioner for his information, and is egregiously misinformed.

Senator Gallinger asked the Secretary: "The other point, as I understand it, that the Grand Army has pressed upon the President and this Department is that in estimating the amount of pension to be allowed the Bureau shall take cognizance of the several disabilities that the soldier may have, and aggregate them, so as to reach a conclusion as to the amount of pension that should be granted. There has been a great deal of contention on that from the Grand Army of the Republic, covering men of 10 or 11 years. Have you any knowledge as to whether or not that is the practice of the Bureau at the present time, or whether the complaint made by the Grand Army is well-founded?"

To this the Secretary replied: "I should not like to give a positive answer, because the details of the practice are properly left with the Commissioner, who can best answer your question."

That is, the Secretary had absolutely no knowledge of any of the practices of the Pension Bureau, and particularly in relation to these special orders, except what he gained by casual conversation with the Commissioner.

Assistant Secretary Davis said substantially the same, and referred the Committee to the Commissioner as to information about combining disabilities. He himself favored raising the limit to widows' incomes to $3.50. But the most pertinent fact was his testimony as to the origin of the idea of a Codification Commission. He said:

"I would merely say that I feel enthusiastic regarding the first suggestion—the of a commission. The Secretary of the Interior spoke with me about it at the beginning of the Summer."

The Secretary of the Interior immediately corrected him, saying:

"The Commissioner of Pensions spoke to me about it before he wrote me on the 26th of July, 1899, a letter making the suggestion of a Commission. I think we are all agreed about its importance. In order to remove all indefiniteness regarding pension legislation and especially the indefiniteness regarding means of support and daily labor."

Here we have it placed beyond doubt that the Commission was a cunning device of Commissioner Evans to put a shield between himself and those who are indignant at his notification of the laws, and to stave off a settlement of the question at least until after the Presidential election.

As we have said before, the veterans have no objection to the Codification Commission per se. They have little interest whether the laws are codified again or not. But they do most strenuously object to having that device be made an answer to their appeals for immediate justice. They resent being amused by an elaborate and cumbrous commission, which will postpone the day of relief until hundreds of thousands of them are in their graves, asking for earthly relief. They demand that plain, mandatory laws now on the statute books, and which have seemed sufficiently clear to much better men than are now in charge of the pension system, shall be executed according to their plain, mandatory terms, and not be juggled with by a man whose main object is to find pretexts for not obeying directions expressed in clear, unmistakable English words.

Situation Discussed with Interest.

Addresses by Capt. J. C. Cunningham, Mr. B. A. Denmark, Mr. J. L. Lester and R. V. Oliver, Esq.—The City Divided Into Fourteen Divisions with Large Committee in Each.

The meeting of the enlarged committee of the Savannah Industrial Association at the Metropolitan Hall last night marked a very decided step forward in the industrial movement. The meeting was not only the largest since the preliminary meeting at the City Exchange, but it was a thoroughly representative one. Better still, those present showed decided interest in the movement and evinced a desire to render aid in every way.

Had it not been announced that no subscriptions would be asked for at this meeting it is very likely that a fine beginning towards securing the desired capital could have been made. One gentleman was heard to remark at the close of the meeting that he would head the list with a subscription for $1,000.

Col. J. L. Lester, chairman of the Committee of Twenty, presided. There were about seventy-five gentlemen present, showing a very satisfactory response to the invitations sent out to become members of the enlarged committee. Others sent letters explaining their absence, some being compelled to be out of the city. Letters of this nature were read by the secretary from B. A. Denmark, Esq., Col. George A. Mercer, Hon. F. Q. Mr. Denmark's letter was received with especial approval by the meeting and is worthy of more general perusal. It is as follows:

I am heartily in accord with the spirit of the association, and will contribute what I can toward its success. Were I present in person I could not say more than this.

Our resources and strength are now taxed to the utmost, and, if I am to be put on any committee to seek subscriptions, I hope it will be the one to call only upon the members of the bar.

In the committee's circular of the 18th it is stated that the claim is made that "thirty-odd factories could be run here at a profit." I do not doubt the statement; indeed, I would not doubt it if the number had been stated to be over one hundred. I trust, however, that those who know what these things are will state them at the meeting tonight, and that the newspapers will educate the public on this line.

I do not believe we have a dead or dying city. There is no reason for the failure of any well managed enterprise in Savannah. There are any quantity of people here ready to invest in any enterprise that will benefit themselves and the public. The great need in these enterprises is to have those in charge who will see to it that they are not failures. This, after all, is the great problem which the association has before it when it has set before the public the enterprises to be engaged in.

Regretting my inability to be present should I not be present—and begging again to express my entire sympathy with the movement in hand, I remain very truly yours, B. A. Denmark.

It was an imposing mansion, too, before which the equipage presently paused and a footman opened the front door and ran briskly down to the sidewalk to assist the travellers alighting. None of her sociates, married or single, lived in equal style, she reflected with a stir of exultation, as she stepped out, between her husband and his lackey.

Mr. Withers' address dampened the rising glow.

"This is our home, my dear. You will find no cause of discomfort with it," he said, in benign patronage, handing her up the noble flight of stone steps.

"Thank you," she replied, coldly. "It is part of the price for which I sold myself," she was meditating. "I must not quarrel with my bargain."

Miss Field met them in the hall, a wasp-like figure, surmounted by a small head. Her neck was bare and crane-like; her face very oval, her skin opaque and chalky; her hair black and shining, the front in long ringlets; her eyes jet beads, that rolled and twinkled incessantly.

"My dear cousin!" she cried, effusively embracing her patron's hand and blinking back an officious tear. "It is like sunshine to have you home again. How are you?"

"Well, thank you, Harriet; or, I should say, in tolerable health," returned Mr. Withers, magnificently condescending. "Allow me to introduce my wife, Mrs. Withers!"

Miss Field swept a furnishing courtesy. Constance, as the truer lady of the two, offered her hand. It was grasped very slightly, and instantly relinquished.

"Charmed to have the honour, I am sure," murmured Miss Field. "I trust I see Mrs. Withers quite well? But you, cousin—did I understand you to intimate that you were indisposed?" with strained solicitude.

"A trifling attack of indigestion, not worth mentioning to any ears except yours, my good nurse."

Miss Field smiled indulgence in this concession to her anxiety, and Constance, who now heard of the "indisposition" for the first time, looked from one to the other in surprised silence.

"Perhaps Mrs. Withers would like to go directly to her apartments?" pursued Harriet, primly, with another courtesy.

"By all means," Mr. Withers replied for her. "As it is, I fear your dinner will have to wait for her, if, as I presume is the case, you are punctual as is your custom."

"Could I fail in promptitude upon this day of all others?" queried Harriet, sentimentally arch, and preceded the bride upstairs.

that relations of a subterranean and ill
ultimate character are often maintained
between representatives of the city and
representatives of these companies by
which the public is plundered. Such illicit
relations do not always involve the pay-
ment of money by the corporations to the
municipal officers; the money is often
paid to those who control the councilmen,
and other methods of influence are em-
ployed. The election expenses of candi-
dates are often paid along with these
secret methods; there is much direct brib-
ery; many who occupy high positions in
society are connected more or less close
ly with this nefarious business. Mayor
Swift, of Chicago, told the precise truth
when he said that most of the bribery of
city councils was the work of representa-
tive citizens.


What are the reasons urged against
public ownership? They all reduce to
this: It is difficult, and perhaps danger-
ous. So it is, but if it is our business
we had better do it, and not shirk it nor any
part of it. Public ownership is no pana-
cea; it will leave us battles to fight and
obstacles to overcome; but the line of
least resistance to righteous rule lies
through the resumption by the people
of those functions of sovereignty which
they have surrendered to private corpora-
tions. The pressure of the traders and
the contractors upon the officials would,
in the words of Albert Shaw, be incompar-
ably less than that which is now brought
to bear by the corporations. We have
now in all our cities millions of money
in the hands of prominent and influential
men who are financially interested in
maintaining weak or bad government be-
cause they could not obtain from intelli-
gent and honest government the kind of
franchises they want. That condition is
abnormal, and the only deliverance from
it is through the municipal ownership of
public service monopolies.
